title: What was PermGen, why did it cause `OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space` (fixed size, hot-deploy class leaks), and how does Metaspace (Java 8+, native memory, classloader-scoped collection) fix it?
shortTitle: What was PermGen and how does Metaspace fix it?

s1_definition.profdef: PermGen, short for the Permanent Generation, was a fixed-size region inside the heap used before Java 8 to store class metadata, interned strings, and static data. Because it had a fixed maximum set by `-XX:MaxPermSize` and lived inside the heap, applications that loaded many classes, especially application servers that hot-deploy and leak old class loaders, would exhaust it and throw `OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space`. Java 8 replaced PermGen with Metaspace, which stores the same class metadata but in native memory, grows automatically by default, and reclaims a class loader's metadata when that loader becomes unreachable, which largely eliminates the old failure.
s1_definition.analogy: PermGen was like a small fixed-size blueprint cabinet built into the corner of National Bank of India's main vault. Every type of form (class) needed its blueprint stored there. The cabinet had a hard size limit, and worse, when an old version of a form was retired during a system upgrade (a redeploy), its blueprint often got stuck in the cabinet instead of being thrown away, so the cabinet slowly filled with obsolete blueprints until it overflowed. Metaspace replaced it with a separate, expandable blueprint room outside the vault that automatically grows as needed and, when an entire form family is retired, throws away all of that family's blueprints at once.
s1_definition.oneliner: PermGen was a fixed-size, in-heap region for class metadata that overflowed on class-loader leaks, and Metaspace fixed it by moving class metadata to auto-growing native memory that is reclaimed per class loader.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** PermGen, short for the Permanent Generation, was a fixed-size region inside the heap used before Java 8 to store class metadata, interned strings, and static data. Because it had a fixed maximum set by `-XX:MaxPermSize` and lived inside the heap, applications that loaded many classes, especially application servers that hot-deploy and leak old class loaders, would exhaust it and throw `OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space`. Java 8 replaced PermGen with Metaspace, which stores the same class metadata but in native memory, grows automatically by default, and reclaims a class loader's metadata when that loader becomes unreachable, which largely eliminates the old failure.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** PermGen was like a small fixed-size blueprint cabinet built into the corner of National Bank of India's main vault. Every type of form (class) needed its blueprint stored there. The cabinet had a hard size limit, and worse, when an old version of a form was retired during a system upgrade (a redeploy), its blueprint often got stuck in the cabinet instead of being thrown away, so the cabinet slowly filled with obsolete blueprints until it overflowed. Metaspace replaced it with a separate, expandable blueprint room outside the vault that automatically grows as needed and, when an entire form family is retired, throws away all of that family's blueprints at once.

**One line to remember:** PermGen was a fixed-size, in-heap region for class metadata that overflowed on class-loader leaks, and Metaspace fixed it by moving class metadata to auto-growing native memory that is reclaimed per class loader.

sections.s2_technical:
Before Java 8, the Permanent Generation was a dedicated area inside the heap that stored class metadata, the runtime constant pool, interned strings in early versions, and static class data. It had its own fixed maximum controlled by `-XX:MaxPermSize`, separate from the main heap size. Because it was fixed and relatively small by default, any application that loaded a large or growing number of classes could fill it. When it filled, you got the distinctive `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space`, which is different from the ordinary heap out-of-memory error and confused many developers because increasing the heap with `-Xmx` did nothing; you had to increase `-XX:MaxPermSize` specifically.

The classic cause was a class-loader leak during hot deployment. Application servers like Tomcat or WebLogic redeploy a web application by creating a new class loader for the new version and discarding the old one. The metadata of the old version's classes should be reclaimed when the old class loader becomes unreachable. But if anything, such as a thread-local, a cached singleton, or a shutdown hook, holds a reference to even one class or object loaded by the old class loader, the entire old class loader and all its classes stay alive. Each redeploy then leaks another full set of class metadata into PermGen, and after enough redeploys PermGen overflows. This made long-lived application servers fragile in exactly the environments banks run.

Java 8 removed PermGen entirely and introduced Metaspace. Metaspace stores the same class metadata, but in native memory outside the Java heap rather than inside it. This changes two things. First, it is not bounded by the heap; by default Metaspace can grow to use available native memory, so the old fixed-ceiling failure does not happen unless you deliberately cap it with `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize`. Second, Metaspace is organized so that all the metadata for a single class loader is grouped together, and when that class loader becomes unreachable and is collected, the garbage collector can release that entire chunk of native memory in one go. This class-loader-scoped reclamation is a much cleaner fit for the load-and-unload pattern.

Metaspace does not magically cure class-loader leaks; if your code still pins an old class loader, its metadata still cannot be freed, and you can get an `OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace` if you have capped it, or you simply grow native memory without bound if you have not. A senior nuance is therefore that Metaspace changes where and how class metadata is managed but does not excuse leaking class loaders, and in practice I still set `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` in production so a leak fails fast and visibly rather than silently consuming all native memory and getting the container OOMKilled. Another nuance is that interned strings moved to the heap in Java 7 already, so by Java 8 Metaspace is essentially class metadata, which makes it easier to reason about.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India ran its core services on an application server and redeployed a new build several times a day. On the old Java 7 runtime, after a dozen redeploys the server threw OutOfMemoryError PermGen space and had to be restarted. This is exactly the PermGen class-loader-leak problem, because each redeploy leaked the old version's class metadata into the fixed-size PermGen.

Problem 2 — After moving to Java 8, the same redeploy pattern no longer crashed the fixed region, because Metaspace lives in native memory and reclaims a class loader's metadata when that loader is collected. This is exactly how Metaspace fixes the issue, and the team set a Metaspace cap so any residual leak fails fast and visibly.

In the mini-project we simulate loading classes with throwaway class loaders to mimic redeploys, show that releasing the loader lets Metaspace reclaim the metadata, and report Metaspace usage before and after. We also show the flags that cap PermGen historically versus Metaspace today.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile the demo
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/metaspace/MetaspaceDemo.java

# Java 8+: Metaspace, native, auto-growing; cap it to fail fast on leaks
java -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=128m -Xlog:gc+metaspace \
     -cp out com.bank.metaspace.MetaspaceDemo

# Historical Java 7 PermGen flags (for contrast; removed in Java 8):
#   java -XX:PermSize=64m -XX:MaxPermSize=128m ...   # PermSize/MaxPermSize gone in 8+
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a startup report, then five simulated redeploys each using a throwaway class loader, then a collection and a final report.

Step 1: At startup the reporter reads the Metaspace memory pool and logs its usage, which already reflects the core JVM and application classes loaded into native memory.

Step 2: Each redeploy iteration creates a new URLClassLoader, loads a class through it, and then lets the loader go out of scope. Loading classes adds their metadata to Metaspace, so usage ticks up during the loop.

Step 3: Because no reference is kept to each throwaway loader, each one becomes unreachable as soon as the iteration ends. This is the crucial difference from the PermGen leak scenario, where something would have pinned the loader.

Step 4: The collection runs and the garbage collector reclaims the unreachable class loaders. Metaspace, organized per class loader, releases each loader's metadata chunk back to native memory in one go.

Step 5: The final report shows Metaspace usage settling rather than climbing without bound, demonstrating class-loader-scoped reclamation. On old PermGen, the same pattern with a leak would have marched steadily toward OutOfMemoryError PermGen space.

```text
[INFO] [startup] Metaspace used = 4200 KB (native memory, auto-grows unless MaxMetaspaceSize set)
[INFO] [after 5 redeploys + GC (loaders released)] Metaspace used = 4320 KB (native memory, auto-grows unless MaxMetaspaceSize set)
[INFO] Metaspace reclaims a loader's class metadata once the loader is unreachable
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  PermGen (Java ≤7)                 Metaspace (Java 8+)
  ──────────────────────           ───────────────────────────
  inside the HEAP                   NATIVE memory (outside heap)
  fixed max: -XX:MaxPermSize        auto-grows; cap MaxMetaspaceSize
  leak path:                        reclaim path:
    redeploy → new loader             redeploy → new loader
    old loader PINNED by                old loader UNREACHABLE
    threadlocal/singleton             │
    → metadata stuck                   ▼
    → PermGen fills                   GC frees whole loader chunk
    → OOM: PermGen space              → Metaspace stable

  redeploy ×5 (throwaway loaders)
    │ each: new URLClassLoader → load class → drop loader
    ▼
  GC → unreachable loaders collected → metadata released
    → Metaspace usage settles (no runaway)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Before Java 8, the Permanent Generation, or PermGen, was a dedicated region inside the heap that stored class metadata, the runtime constant pool, and static class data. Its defining characteristic was that it had its own fixed maximum, set with the MaxPermSize flag, separate from the main heap. Because it was fixed and fairly small by default, any application that loaded a large or growing number of classes could fill it, and when it filled you got the distinctive out-of-memory error for PermGen space. What confused people was that raising the heap with dash Xmx did nothing for this error; you specifically had to raise MaxPermSize.

The classic cause was a class-loader leak during hot deployment. Application servers redeploy a web application by creating a brand new class loader for the new version and discarding the old one, and the metadata of the old version's classes should be reclaimed once the old class loader becomes unreachable. But if anything at all, such as a thread-local, a cached singleton, or a shutdown hook, holds a reference to even one class loaded by that old loader, the entire old class loader and all of its classes stay alive. Each redeploy then leaks another full set of class metadata into PermGen, and after enough redeploys PermGen overflows. That made long-lived application servers fragile exactly in the always-on environments banks run.

Java 8 removed PermGen and replaced it with Metaspace, which stores the same class metadata but in native memory outside the heap rather than inside it. This fixes the old failure in two ways. First, Metaspace is not bounded by the heap and by default grows to use available native memory, so the fixed-ceiling failure simply does not occur unless I deliberately cap it with MaxMetaspaceSize. Second, Metaspace groups all the metadata for a single class loader together, so when that class loader becomes unreachable and is collected, the garbage collector can release that entire chunk of native memory in one operation, which is a clean fit for the load-and-unload pattern of redeploys.

The honest senior nuance I always add is that Metaspace does not cure class-loader leaks. If my code still pins an old class loader, its metadata still cannot be freed, and I will either get an out-of-memory error for Metaspace if I capped it, or I will grow native memory without bound and get the container OOMKilled if I did not. So in production I deliberately set MaxMetaspaceSize, because I would much rather a residual leak fail fast and visibly with a clear Metaspace error than silently eat all the native memory. In short, Metaspace changed where and how class metadata is managed, moving it to auto-growing native memory with per-class-loader reclamation, but the discipline of not leaking class loaders still matters.

---

keyPoints: PermGen: fixed-size memory for class metadata (pre-Java 8)
OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space — common with many class loads (app servers)
Metaspace (Java 8+): uses native memory, grows automatically
No fixed upper limit by default — set with -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize if needed
Fix: Metaspace eliminates PermGen OOM, but monitor for classloader leaks
